  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent service, foster
  growth and opportunity, and create a joyous and collaborative environment.

  LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

  1. Adopting a resolution declaring a Local Emergency resulting from the Windstorm

  Manager’s Administrative Declaration of Emergency dated January 16, 2025,

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
On January 7, 2025, Los Angeles and Ventura Counties experienced severe wind events
and devastating fires that caused widespread damage to private and public property in
local communities leaving infrastructure, buildings, and roads damaged or destroyed. The
events also resulted in power outages, downed trees, and significant debris. Locally, the
City of Monterey Park (“City”) was impacted by these events resulting in the need of
immediate response from City employees and contractors. While City employees
continue to assess the impacts from these events, the Public Works Director (“Director”)
and Fire Chief (“Chief”) identified risks to City operations and emergency responses. The
Director and Chief recommend that the City Council adopt a resolution ratifying the City
Manager’s administrative declaration of emergency regarding the recent wind events and
fires to protect public health, safety, and general welfare.

BACKGROUND:

The unprecedented catastrophe resulting from the Windstorm and Firestorms throughout
the Greater Los Angeles Region prompted the City Manager to declare a local emergency
on January 16, 2025. This action was desirable for several different reasons including,
without limitation, the following:

  •  The widespread structure destruction and damage will result in increased prices
  for construction products and contractor services. Expediting the City’s ability to
  secure contracts for capital improvement projects is in the public interest. Many of
  the approved public works projects are intended to improve vital infrastructure such
  as water, stormwater, and wastewater facilities.

  •  The Governor’s Executive Order dated January 12, 2025, directs state agencies
  to streamline building approvals. It is in the public interest for the City to jumpstart
  that process to assist with developers seeking to build within the City’s jurisdiction.

  •  Fire prevention is always critical. The current emergency, however, starkly
  emphasized the immediate need to exercise the City’s police powers to protect
  public health and safety. This, among other things, includes undergrounding power
  lines to the greatest extent practicable.

  •  The City expended public resources (personnel, equipment, gas, etc.) while
  assisting neighboring jurisdictions during this emergency. It is in the public interest
  for the City to seek reimbursement from federal and state agencies for these costs.

As to public works projects, the widespread destruction of structures will reduce the
available contractors in the region. This will likely further increase the cost of construction
for all projects including, without limitation, public works projects previously approved by
the City Council via the capital improvement plan (“CIP”). It is vital that the City take
immediate action to secure contractors needed to complete the CIP as many of these
projects involve improvements to critical infrastructure within the City including, without
limitation, water infrastructure necessary for firefighting.

Ordinarily, the Public Works Department would schedule bidding in accordance with the
Public Contract Code (“PCC”) to complete CIP projects. However, the risk of price
gouging and availability of resources poses a local risk to the City’s ability to complete
infrastructure repairs and improvements through its regular contracting procedures.
Consequently, the inability to complete some of these projects in a timely manner could
threaten public health and safety.

The wind events and ongoing fires demonstrate the need for a proactive approach in
mitigating and preventing such tragedies. The Eaton Canyon fire was started as a result
of overhead power lines coming into contact with vegetation. As of the writing of this
report, the fire has resulted in 16 fatalities, destroyed over 4,500 structures, and is
approximately 45% contained.2 The undergrounding power lines through underground
utility districts can significantly reduce the risk of fires with downed power lines.

The establishment of an Underground Utility District on Monterey Pass Road between W.
Garvey Avenue and Vagabond Drive was approved by City Council on July 20, 2022.
This project would be the City's fourth major Rule 20A undergrounding project since 1968.
Monterey Pass Road is a major North-West collector through the City of Monterey Park
that carries a significant volume of traffic. The estimated cost for the undergrounding is
$6.8 million as provided in the Preliminary Rough Order of Magnitude Cost Estimate by
SCE. Under Rule 20A, each utility company, at its own expense, is required to
underground its overhead facilities within the public right-of-way and up to 100 feet on
private property. The affected utility companies include SCE, AT&T, Frontier, Verizon
Wireless, Time Warner and Crown Castle.

It is anticipated that the undergrounding of utilities on Monterey Pass Road will
significantly reduce the risks of a major fire in the City. Five of the property owners in the
affected area on Monterey Pass Road have been entirely unresponsive to the City’s
efforts.

If adopted, the Resolution would ratify the City Manager’s decision to issue an emergency
order to abate a public nuisance on approximately five properties where the property
owners are either non-responsive or non-cooperative. The abatement would include,
without limitation, securing a public utility easement upon these properties to allow
installation of underground power lines.

While the City continues to assess the impacts of current and future events, the proposed
Resolution will address risks to reduce the magnitude of negative impacts to the
community and help in the preservation of public health and safety. As cleanup continues
from the devastating winds and fires, local, regional and state governments continue to
estimate damage costs. The City of Monterey Park is no different and will be seeking
reimbursement for its response to the events. The Chief, Police Chief, and Director
recommend that City Council adopt the proposed resolution which would allow staff to
seek reimbursement for the cleanup efforts and damages sustained during these events.

  The City Council does resolve as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds and declares as follows:

  A.  Conditions of extreme peril to the safety of persons exist following the
  Governor’s Proclamation of Emergency dated January 7, 2025 due to the
  Palisades Fire, Eaton Canyon Fire, and windstorm conditions (the “LA
  Emergency”).

  B.  The fires causing the LA Emergency have collectively burned more than
  40,000 acres, devastating communities throughout the Greater Los Angeles
  Basin by destroying or damaging more than 12,000 structures.

  C.  Reports from the City Manager, the Fire Chief, and Police Chief confirm that
  the City expending multiple public resources to help mitigate the effects of
  the LA Emergency including, without limitation, providing equipment,
  personnel, and mobilization throughout the Greater Los Angeles Basin.

  D.  The destruction of homes by the fires burning in Los Angeles and Ventura
  Counties will reduce the available contractors in the region, which is likely
  to further increase the cost of construction for all projects including, without
  limitation, public works projects previously approved by the City Council via
  the capital improvement plan (“CIP”).

  E.  It is vital that the City take immediate action to secure contractors needed
  to complete the CIP as many of these projects involve improvements to
  critical infrastructure within the City including, without limitation, water
  infrastructure necessary for firefighting.

  F.  Assessing the totality of the circumstances, the City Manager declared a
  local emergency effective January 16, 2025 (“Local Emergency”). A copy of
  the Local Emergency is attached as exhibit “A,” and incorporated by
  reference (“Emergency Declaration”).

  upon a four-fifths vote, declare that public interest and necessity demand

  or replace a public facility, take any directly related and immediate action
  required by that emergency, and procure the necessary equipment,
  services, and supplies for those purposes, without giving notice for bids to
  let contracts.

J.  The circumstances of the Local Emergency prompted the City Manager, in
  consultation with the Fire Chief, to identify various methods to reduce the
  immediate threat of fires within the City’s jurisdiction and avoid exasperating
  the LA Emergency.

K.  One preventative measure is to underground power lines within the City.
  Such a project is currently underway for the MPR District established by
  Resolution No. 2022-R71, adopted August 17, 2022. Implementing the
  undergrounding contemplated by the MPR District is an essential feature
  for fire prevention (see, e.g., Memorandum dated January 16, 2025 from
  Fire Chief Chris Thompson) and is reflected in Southern California Edison’s
  (“SCE”) policy to proactively turn off power during high wind events such as
  the LA Emergency (see, e.g., Quantitative and Qualitative Factors for PSPS
  Decision-Making [SCE; Rev. November 6, 2023]).

L.  The circumstances of the LA Emergency and Local Emergency emphasize
  the immediate need to protect public health and safety by undergrounding
  power lines expeditiously for fire prevention.

M.  SCE and the Public Works Director have repeatedly attempted to secure
  the voluntary cooperation of properties to underground power lines within
  the MPR District. They report challenges from owners of real property

  undergrounding power lines. The location of these Nuisance Properties are
  set forth in the Order for Urgency Abatement in attached Exhibit “B,” which
  is incorporated by reference (“Abatement Order”).

  DECLARATION OF LOCAL EMERGENCY

The City Manager finds:

Following the Governor’s Proclamation of Emergency dated January 7, 2025 due
to the Palisades Fire and windstorm conditions (the “LA Emergency”), and
subsequent Executive Orders (e.g., EO N-4-25 dated January 12, 2025), I find a
local emergency to exist within the City of Monterey Park effective January 16,
2025 (“Local Emergency”) pursuant to Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) §
2.52.060(a)(1).

The fires causing the LA Emergency have collectively burned more than 40,000
acres, devastating communities throughout the Greater Los Angeles Basin by
destroying or damaging more than 12,000 structures. Initial estimates suggest that
the resulting economic impact will exceed $200 billion making the LA Emergency
the most destructive in California history and, potentially, the United States.

The destruction of homes by the fires burning in Los Angeles and Ventura Counties
will reduce the available contractors in the region, which is likely to further increase
the cost of construction for all projects including, without limitation, public works
projects previously approved by the City Council via the capital improvement plan
(“CIP”). It is vital that the City take immediate action to secure contractors needed
to complete the CIP as many of these projects involve improvements to critical
infrastructure within the City including, without limitation, water infrastructure
necessary for firefighting. A list of the approved CIP is attached as Exhibit “A,” and
incorporated by reference. The Public Works Director is directed to take all steps
needed to secure contractors to complete the projects identified within the CIP.
Additionally, the City Attorney is requested to assist in completing such tasks
through all legal means.

On January 12, 2025, the Governor issued Executive Order N-4-25 (the “EO”).
Among other things, the EO mandates that State agencies:

  1. “review and provide a report to [the Governor] with recommendations
  regarding any provision of the [California] Building Standards Code,
  Title 24 of the California Code of Regulations, that should be
  suspended for projects … in order to facilitate rapid, safe, and cost-
  effective rebuilding and recovery.”

  2. “coordinate with local governments to identify and recommend
  procedures, including but not limited to exploring the use of pre-
  approved plans and waivers of certain permitting requirements, to
  Page 15 of 33
   establish rapid permitting and approval processes to expedite the
  reconstruction or replacement of residential properties destroyed or
  damaged by fire. The recommended procedures shall have the
  ultimate goal of issuing all necessary permits and approvals within
  30 days.”

The Planning Director is directed to identify and recommend regulations within the
MPMC that will help fulfill the EO’s intent and present those findings to the City

The Finance Director, in coordination with the Fire Chief and the Police Chief, is

and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (“FEMA”) technical expertise,
resources, and financial assistance. The City Attorney is requested to assist in
completing such tasks through all legal means.

  The City Council of the city of Monterey Park does resolve as follows:

SECTION 1: Planning Agency. Pursuant to Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) §
2.56.020(B), the City Council is the Monterey Park Planning Agency for purposes of this
Resolution. On August 17, 2022, the City Council adopted Resolution No. 2022-R69 to
allow an emergency response to recurring water main leaks within the Monterey Pass
Road between Vagabond Drive and Brightwood Street (“Emergency Project”). The
Emergency Project was not previously included within the Capital Improvement Plan
(“CIP”) as approved by Resolution No. 2022-R32 on May 4, 2022. To ensure that the CIP
includes the Emergency Project in accordance with Government Code § 65401, the City
Council amends Resolution No. 2022-R32 to add the Emergency Project. Pursuant to
Government Code § 65103(C), the City Council finds that the CIP, as amended by adding
the Emergency Project, is consistent with the Monterey Park General Plan. Among other
things the CIP meets the following goals in the General Plan:

  •  Goal 2.0 of the Circulation Element: Provide a local street system that
  accommodates current and future traffic volumes;

  •  Goal 5.0 of the Circulation Element: Create and maintain a connected
  system of bicycle routes and pedestrian facilities that meets the need of City
  residents;

  •  Goal 6.0 of the Circulation Element: Ensure that all development projects
  provide well-designed parking facilities that are safe, convenient, and
  attractive;

  •  Goal 3.0 of the Safety and Community Services Element: Protect public and
  private properties from geologic hazards associated with steep slopes,
  unstable hillsides, and liquefaction-prone areas;

  •  Goal 13.0 of the Safety and Community Services Element: Provide
  adequate sewer, water, and drainage systems to meet the needs of City
  residents and businesses; and

  •  Goal 4.0 of the Resources Element: Conserve and protect groundwater
  supply and water resources.

immunities set forth in Government Code § 830.6 regarding the plans and construction of
the Emergency Project. Accordingly, in addition to the other projects in the CIP, the City
Council authorizes the City Engineer to exercise discretionary approval for plans or

  ORDER FOR URGENCY ABATEMENT

The City Manager finds:

Following the Governor’s Proclamation of Emergency dated January 7, 2025 due
to the Palisades Fire and windstorm conditions (the “LA Emergency”), and
subsequent Executive Orders (e.g., EO N-4-25 dated January 12, 2025), I
declared a local emergency pursuant to Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”)
§ 2.52.060(a)(1) to exist within the City of Monterey Park effective January 16,
2025 (“Local Emergency”).

In implementing the Local Emergency, I am informed by the Fire Chief and the
Public Works Director that owners of real properties located at 500, 524, 573, 598
and 665 Monterey Pass Road are refusing to cooperate with the City and Southern
California Edison (“SCE”) in undergrounding power lines (“Nuisance Properties”).
As stated in the declaration from Fire Chief Chris Thompson (dated January 16,
2025), undergrounding power lines is an essential feature for fire prevention.
SCE’s policy in proactively turning off power during high wind events such as the
LA Emergency is directly related to fire hazards resulting from downed overhead
power lines.

SCE and the Public Works Director have repeatedly attempted to secure the
voluntary cooperation of the Nuisance Properties to underground the power lines.
The circumstances of the LA Emergency emphasize the immediate need to protect
public health and safety by undergrounding power lines expeditiously for fire
prevention. Allowing the Nuisance Properties to imperil neighboring properties –
and the greater Monterey Park community – is unconscionable and constitutes an
imminent threat to public health and safety.

Consequently, I am utilizing Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) § 4.30.180
to abate the public nuisances on the Nuisance Properties on an urgency basis.
The Fire Chief and Public Works Director are directed to take all steps needed to
ensure that the power lines servicing the Nuisance Properties are undergrounded
in accordance with SCE’s Rule 20A plans and specifications for that District.
Additionally, the City Attorney is requested to assist such urgency abatement
efforts and to take all legal action necessary under this Order for Urgency
Abatement.

SUBJECT:  Infrastructure Improvements – Underground Power Lines

As seen most recently with the January 2025 Eaton and Palisades Fires, brush fire risks
continue to escalate due to climate change and urban expansion. Given the severity of
the most recent fires, it is imperative to prioritize the safety and reliability of our electrical
infrastructure. Transitioning to underground power lines in brush fire-prone areas offers
significant benefits that warrant serious consideration:

  1. Fire Risk Mitigation:
  Overhead power lines are a known source of ignition during high wind events and
  dry conditions. Fallen lines or equipment failure can easily spark fires, making
  underground lines a safer alternative in areas at high risk of brush fires.
  2. Enhanced Reliability:
  Underground power lines are far less susceptible to damage from weather
  conditions, such as windstorms or falling tree limbs, which frequently disrupt
  overhead lines. This increases the reliability of power supply, especially during
  extreme weather conditions.
  3. Public Safety:
  By reducing the likelihood of power lines igniting fires, underground systems
  contribute to the safety of residents, emergency responders, and wildlife in affected
  regions.
  4. Long-Term Cost Efficiency:
  Although the initial installation costs for underground power lines are higher, they
  reduce the long-term financial burden associated with maintenance, repairs, and
  fire-related liabilities.
  5. Environmental and Aesthetic Benefits:
  Underground power lines eliminate the visual impact of overhead lines, preserving
  the natural landscape. Additionally, they reduce the need for vegetation
  management around poles and wires.
  6. Support for Resilient Communities:
  As part of broader efforts to build climate-resilient infrastructure, underground
  power lines align with sustainability goals and provide communities with
  dependable energy systems during crises.

power lines in high-risk areas far outweigh the challenges. Implementing this change
demonstrates a proactive approach to safeguarding lives, property, and the environment.

  property in local communities leaving infrastructure, buildings, and roads damaged
  or destroyed. The events also resulted in power outages, downed trees, and
  significant debris. Locally, the City of Monterey Park (“City”) was impacted by these
  events resulting in the need of immediate response from City employees and
  contractors. While City employees continue to assess the impacts from these
  events, the Public Works Director (“Director”) and Fire Chief (“Chief”) identified
  risks to City operations and emergency responses. The Director and Chief
  recommend that the City Council adopt a resolution ratifying the City Manager’s
  administrative declaration of emergency regarding the recent wind events and fires
  to protect public health, safety, and general welfare.

  CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
  The Resolution itself and the actions anticipated by the Resolution were reviewed
  pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code §§
  21000, et seq., “CEQA”) and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal.
  Code of Regulations §§15000, et seq., the “CEQA Guidelines”). Based upon that
  review, this action is exempt from further review pursuant to CEQA Guidelines §
  15269(a) because the protection of public and private property is necessary to
  maintain service essential to the public, health and welfare.

  Action Taken: The City Council adopted Resolution No. 2025-R3 declaring a local
  emergency resulting from the windstorm and firestorm events identified on or about
  January 7, 2025, ratifying the City Manager’s administrative Declaration of
  Emergency dated January 16, 2025, ratifying the City Manager’s Order for
  Urgency Abatement, and authorizing the City Manager to directly negotiate
  contracts pursuant to Public Contract Code §§ 20168 and 2205 and authorized the
  Public Works Director to approve change orders and contingency as appropriate
  up to 15% of the contract amount for these projects.
